title: The Impact of Generative AI Applications on Student Learning Outcomes in Science Education: A Systematic Review
venue: Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH)
extended_summary:
This paper asks what effects generative artificial intelligence (GAI) applications have on student learning outcomes in science education, with a particular focus on middle-school science. The authors conducted a systematic literature review to synthesize evidence from recent studies on AI-supported science learning, including chatbot-based learning, AI-assisted game-based learning, virtual reality-enhanced science learning, intelligent tutoring systems, image recognition technologies, AI robots, and AI-driven digital modules.

The review searched Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and TRDizin, using PRISMA procedures and inclusion criteria that limited studies to recent experimental or quasi-experimental research in science education. Although the paper’s overall aim is broad, the included studies mostly involved students in grades 5–9, with many studies centered on middle school and some including elementary and high-school learners. The context is science classrooms and science learning environments, often with technology-enhanced or blended digital instruction.

Across the 12 included studies, the authors conclude that GAI tools generally improve academic achievement, conceptual understanding, scientific and digital literacy, personalized learning opportunities, motivation, participation, self-efficacy, and other affective outcomes. They also emphasize that these tools can support inquiry, reflection, and inclusivity, especially when adapted to learner needs and cultural context. The paper argues that AI should be integrated into science education in ethically sound, pedagogically informed ways, alongside greater teacher AI literacy and future long-term research.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review with PRISMA screening, but it is not a meta-analysis and the included studies are mostly quasi-experimental with heterogeneous outcomes. The review synthesizes evidence qualitatively rather than providing pooled estimates, so methodological certainty is moderate rather than high.
impact_tier_rationale: The review describes modest-to-meaningful positive effects across academic achievement, scientific literacy, and motivation in middle-school science contexts. Because the paper does not provide pooled effect sizes, the impact is best treated as promising but not yet quantified at a blue-tier level.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of generative AI chatbots and conversational agents used for middle-school science learning, including ChatGPT-style support, rule-based chatbots, and inquiry bots for guided scientific inquiry and concept learning.
Intelligent tutoring system applications integrated with augmented reality to support personalized middle-school science instruction and feedback.
AI-assisted game-based learning, VR-enhanced science learning, and other simulation-based science activities used to improve conceptual understanding and engagement.
AI robot image-recognition learning activities in science classes, used as an embodied/robotic support for concept learning and motivation.
AI-assisted personalized science learning environments that adapt tasks, pacing, or learning paths to student needs, including culturally responsive interactive digital modules.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 12-study synthesis, generative AI applications were associated with improved science learning outcomes, especially academic achievement and conceptual understanding. Reported effects included higher achievement in AI-supported groups, better understanding of cell division and other science concepts, and improved scientific literacy; however, the review does not report a pooled effect size because it is a narrative systematic review rather than a meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Academic achievement tests, conceptual understanding assessments, scientific literacy measures

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI-supported science learning was linked to higher motivation, interest, engagement, participation, self-efficacy, and perceived competence. Examples in the included studies noted increased motivation in experimental groups, greater willingness to interact, and improved participation in AI-supported and AR/ITS settings, but no pooled quantitative estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Motivation surveys, engagement/participation indicators, self-efficacy/perceived competence measures

finding.finding_summary: The review reports gains in higher-order skills such as scientific literacy, critical evaluation of claims, inquiry skills, and metacognitive reflection. For example, students using chatbot-based inquiry systems could review chat histories to reflect on prior reasoning, while ChatGPT-supported socio-scientific text activities prompted some students to question climate claims, though critical evaluation remained challenging for many.
finding.measure: Scientific literacy tasks, inquiry skill indicators, claim evaluation/reflection evidence
